principles.title: Research First, Research Often
principles.body: Utilize research for identifying new opportunities and keep learning throughout a project's lifecycle using appropriate research methodologies based on project constraints, timelines, and learning objectives.

principles.title: Incremental Changes
principles.body: Design towards a future without waiting for it. Provide value to users with small improvements over time.

principles.title: Cultivate Collaboration
principles.body: Every team member's voice is valuable. Work hard to build relationships, encourage engagement from others, and bring them along for the ride.

principles.title: Consider Your Audience
principles.body: Curate communications based on who's listening. Find the right story to tell in an engaging way that is unique to your audience.

principles.title: Be Holistic
principles.body: Individual user tasks are often inter-connected. Consider the total impact across product feature teams and all platform areas when making design decisions.

principles.title: Evolve and Be Slushee
principles.body: Reflect, evaluate, and always be changing. Experiment with new processes to improve and optimize team collaboration and effectiveness.

projects.title: Customer Segmentation
projects.description: Led a customer segmentation initiative post-merger (Upright + Neatoscan) to define segments, representative customers, and needs maps, enabling better product decision-making, cohort analysis, and roadmap planning.
projects.detail: Built a scalable segmentation model for ~250 customers using a mix of quantitative “self-sorting” reports and collaborative qualitative sorting to define segment criteria, characteristics, and representative customers for feature logging and product strategy.

sections.content: Formerly competing companies, Upright Labs and Neatoscan merged in 2023. The merger kick started a product team-led investigation into the market offering across the two companies. The goal was to identify complementary and competitive features. Research into the customer base to identify themes in their structure, behavior, usage, and needs was also tasked to the product team. I led this customer segmentation project. The project involved categorizing our customers, identifying their primary needs, and evaluating the effectiveness of our total products and how well our products were meeting the needs of our customers.

image.alt: Goal mapping diagrams for several customer segments, showing shared and unique goals across each group

content: Identify key attributes that define our customers across Upright and Neatoscan
Surface themes shared across customers and group individual customers into segments
Document critical data about each segment and their unique goals, needs, and challenges
A defined list of unique customer segments
Documented characteristics of each customer segment
Selected “representative customer” for each customer segment to use in feature logging
Mapped needs diagrams for each customer segment

sections.content: The goal was not to individually map all 250 Upright and Neatoscan customers to defined customer segments, but to use data on our customers to create the criteria and characteristics of each segment.

content: Identify attributes (properties) to use in the classification of customer segments — for example, e-commerce team size, top key performance indicators, and channels
Leverage attributes (properties) to group customers into segments
Define goals, needs, and challenges for each unique customer segment

sections.content:
With 250 customers across Upright and Neatoscan, the most efficient approach was to use quantitative data points with a single report that would “self-sort” the full customer list into initial groups. This became the “genus” — the family — grouping.

The larger family groups were then further broken down using qualitative attributes, defining the narrower groups of the “species.” This process allowed for individual tracking of all attributes across the entire client list while also making the process more precise than self-assigning customers to a categorized segment.

sections.subheading: Step one: Quantitative self-sorting into genus groups
content: Two reports, separating Upright and Neatoscan into individual reports, returned each customer's data alongside: e-commerce team size, average number of items listed per month, and average monthly revenue (used for auto-sorting)
Additional attributes surfaced further themes: average support volume and duration (Upright only), top 3 item types by volume, and channels

Auto-sorted groups were determined by team size, then split into a high- or low-“performance” sub-category based on average revenue per team member — for example, a team of 1 earning under $10,000 per team member would be marked Extra Small / Low

image.alt: Quantitative genus grouping report used to auto-sort the customer list

sections.content: Shared customer organizations (those overlapping between Upright and Neatoscan) were evaluated individually to see the variation in reported values. Where there was a wide delta between the data, we took the average between the two companies' attribute values.

A small group from Upright's Services, CS, and Growth teams took the broad genus groupings and sorted them into narrower customer segments (“species”), using their firsthand knowledge of each organization. Sorting started by identifying any “snowflake” organizations, then participants used a matrix to group and plot customers by e-commerce experience and change adoption — nine groups emerged from the activity. A similar exercise was run separately with the Neatoscan team using their accessible qualitative attributes.

image.alt: Collaborative sorting session matrix used to group customers by e-commerce experience and change adoption

sections.content: The remaining qualitative attributes (top KPIs, main value proposition, facility size, sale approach, organization model, and organization type) were layered onto the nine initial customer segments to identify any additional unique groupings. The final list of customer segments was documented along with each segment's shared characteristics and one “representative customer” to be used in feature logging.

image.alt: Final customer segment groupings after layering additional qualitative attributes

sections.subheading: Attributes Glossary and User Role List
sections.content: A companion glossary documents the full definitions behind every attribute and user role used throughout the classification and sorting process.

The final defined customer segments were designed to better interpret product performance metrics when measuring the success of new features and surfacing new opportunities. The product team is able to create data cohorts (within Amplitude) based on the defined customer segments to get a more granular view of product data.

Customer segments now inform conversation and decision-making in several ways:

image.alt: Customer segment cohort view used for product data reporting

gallery.alt: Goal mapping and needs pairing example for the customer segment: “New and Resistant”
gallery.caption: Goal mapping and needs pairing example for the customer segment: “New and Resistant”

content: Ensure feature logging has a diverse sample of customer organizations without needing to individually evaluate every organization — how might we define a “representative customer” from each segment to further analyze product usage, feature logging, and workflow documentation?

Evolve our products to be more flexible and accommodating to a variety of organization types with unique workflows and needs — how might we optimize our products to fit the needs of a spectrum of users?
Granularly define the audience for new product features — how might we balance new features across our diverse customer set?
Increase data-driven inputs when evaluating product prioritization and new opportunities — how might we leverage customer segments to help plan product roadmaps?
Take a scalable, personalized approach to supporting our customers — how might our playbooks evolve when considering the unique qualities of a customer?
Onboard new customers efficiently — how might we leverage the defined criteria to classify new customers and optimize our internal onboarding process?
Granularly track feature adoption and establish cohorts for product reporting — how might we create and maintain customer cohorts to analyze product data?

projects.title: Conveyor Workflow
projects.description: Concepted a conveyor-based stationary picking workflow in Lister to speed up apparel fulfillment, reduce errors, and keep shipping cycles under one day for high-volume clothing operations.
projects.detail: Designed and documented an end-to-end stationary conveyor picking workflow for apparel orders (including bulk actions, order locking, and a cycled fulfillment screen), with assumptions, edge cases, and success metrics to support a customer pilot.

sections.heading: Background and Context
sections.content:
Select customers are interested in installing two clothing conveyors. The conveyors allow for the convent storage and picking of apparel items. Customer organizations hope to increase clothing order fulfillment efficiency with the conveyor system. The conveyor can be triggered to deliver any piece of clothing when sent a request for a given location. A picking workflow needs to be designed allowing users in Lister to pick clothing items using this conveyor.

More on conveyors: https://www.white-conveyors.com/market-dryclean.php

sections.heading: Open questions
content: What's the current picking process/workflow for orgs that are not utilizing Link for digital picking? How does picking from Lister currently work? — A: Users multi-select from the orders page and print pack slips that travel to the locations with the picker and then travel to shipping with the item, or (in an extreme use case) users pick from an SGW pick list

What might be a plausible equipment setup for GW Minneapolis given their existing space? Is it possible to place a workstation (or two) directly by the conveyors? Is GW Minneapolis interested in combining picking and shipping for single item, clothing orders? Would a conveyor workstation need to double as a “put away station” as well?
How will locations for conveyors be set up in Lister? What might the naming convention look like — for example, Conveyor 01 - Space 001, Conveyor 02 - Space 239?
What about orders that are mixed type (clothing and collectibles)? Should we limit to single item orders? — A: Separate workflows based on order type
What happens when an item is not found?
What happens when the wrong item is in the location?
How might we ensure orders are locked and unavailable to other pickers?

If “picking” multiple orders at one time, would it be faster to cycle through locations in order and match to pack slips, or pick items based on the orders? How fast do the conveyors cycle through the full locations? Are the conveyors multi-directional (do they travel forwards and backwards)?
Are clothing items that are stored on a conveyor barcoded?
How are items attached to the conveyor? — A: Hangers, unsure on type
Will the conveyors be using the “Automated Order Assembly System” and White system software?

sections.heading: Assumptions
content: a computer workstation with Lister and a scanner will be directly next to the output of the conveyor
GW Minneapolis will NOT be using a conveyor with an automated order assembly system
all clothing items stored on the conveyors are barcoded and the conveyor location has been applied to each item
GW Minneapolis could potentially be picking, packing, and shipping clothing in a single station but will not be at launch of the new conveyor picking workflow
a left and right, separate systems for each conveyor, is less taxing mentally when fulfilling orders for users
picking single and multi-item orders separately is less taxing mentally when fulfilling orders for users and will reduce errors
Lister can send multiple triggers to conveyor based on user action and queued location IDs

sections.heading: User Stories
sections.content:
Stationary Picker/Shipper Role

As a picker/shipper dedicated to conveyor-stored clothing…

I want to quickly and accurately fulfill clothing-specific orders…

So I can meet my picking (and shipping goals) while also mitigating customer returns based on fulfillment errors.

sections.heading: Objectives
content: send location of items ready to fulfill to conveyor to retrieve items from location
allow user to select orders to pick targeting category, type, and/or location
help users ensure that orders are fulfilled accurately
potentially: create a onestep process for picking, packing, and shipping for clothing items on stored on conveyors

sections.heading: Hypothesis
sections.content:
We believe that if we create a system and workflow for “stationary pickers” to quickly and accurately pick clothing orders, and potentially pack and ship orders at one station …  

will achieve a super efficient workflow for organizations handling large clothing orders making the total fulfillment time drop significantly …

We will know we are successful when the average fulfillment time of organizations utilizing the conveyor workflow will reduce overtime and shipping cycles (from time of payment through shipping label created) will be maintained under a day for clothing orders.

sections.heading: Success Metrics
content: Reduce fulfillment times (from pick to pack) for clothing orders
Maintain or reduce customer return metrics with reason “wrong item shipped”
Shipping cycle (from time of payment through shipping label created) ≤ 1 day

sections.heading: Potential Areas to Explore
content: Pick one order at a time
Pick list for targeted locations
Automated picking based on selected orders (”on the fly” pick list from Lister)
Fully automated based on order quantity
Lightest Lift: manually enter location from printed pick list

sections.heading: Initial Concept
sections.content:
Bulk Action within Orders Manager with Cycled Order Fulfillment Screen

A new action within the bulk actions menu in the order manager automates a location list sent to the conveyor to retrieve stored items. Users leverage printed pack slips to verify the item picked against the printed order pack slip.

content: Open Orders Manager
Filter orders by single item order
Filter orders by location = conveyor 1
Multi-select 3–5 single item orders in conveyor 1 locations
Select bulk action: “print pack slips and pick orders”
Place printed pack slips on left side of workstation
Change location filter to = conveyor 2
Multi-select 3–5 single item orders in conveyor 2 locations

Select bulk action: “print pack slips and pick orders” — automated tasks: orders are set to “locked,” locations are sent to the conveyor in order of the printed pack slips, and the “Cycled Order Fulfillment Screen” opens
Place printed pack slips on right side of workstation
Conveyors automatically cycle through locations based on the sequence of the printed pack slips (by selected order)

When the conveyor stops, visually confirm the item against the pack slip, then scan the item barcode to confirm and mark as picked — automated task: when an item is marked as picked (or missing), the system cycles to the next order's location
Attach the pack slip to the item or item hanger
Place the picked order on the rolling clothing rack
Repeat for each order until the cycle is completed
Select another batch of orders

image.alt: Proposed floor configuration with two conveyors and a shared workstation

sections.heading: Functionality Needs
content: New bulk action that is location specific
Parent location selection
“Review style” workflow for confirming/picking orders in lister
Sending location to conveyor based on order

sections.heading: Edge Cases to Consider
content: missing item (nothing in conveyor location)
wrong item in location
item matches pack slip but wrong barcode
correct barcode but item does not match pack slip title/description/image
Challenge assumptions by speaking to Services team members
Test the assumption/hypothesis of separate left and right conveyor operation
Work with the Services team to formalize the recommended operational workflow, including workstation needs, placement in proximity to the conveyor, and shipping needs
Pilot the workflow with an organization with newly purchased conveyors and stress test the recommended workflow
Make adjustments to the workflow based on pilot feedback

projects.title: Flag Do Not Send Items
projects.description: Designed a manifest-stage feedback loop that flags “do not send” items via fuzzy title matching, helping reduce e-commerce rejection rates without disrupting in-store workflow.
projects.detail: Improved inventory quality for e-commerce by introducing a flagged-items table and confirmation flow during manifest creation, using fuzzy matching against an admin-defined “do not send” list while letting sorters continue their normal process.

sections.heading: Background and Context
sections.content: E-commerce teams were facing a challenges regarding inventory quality and volume. Many of the items being sent to e-commerce from store locations were not meeting the requirements for acceptance in selling online. Despite organizations leveraging functionality to call out items not to send to e-commerce, many items were still being returned to stores and not sold through e-commerce. E-commerce teams have a dependency on store locations to create a strong product flow but lack tools to provide feedback to store team members.

image.alt: Empty manifest table before any items are added

sections.heading: User Stories
sections.content:
Sorter/Manifest Creator

As an in-store sorter and manifest creator who is itemizing products to send to the e-commerce team …

I want to quickly and accurately describe each item and only manifest and send items that are of value for e-commerce …

so I can meet or exceed my accepted rate goals for the month and ensure that my store is contributing positively to the revenue goals of our organization.

sections.heading: Objectives
content: help educate store location teams in sorting and manifests creation on items that are not recommended for selling online
automatically “fuzzy match” manifest item title with the existing keywords outlined in the “do not send list”
make manifest creators aware when a manifested item potentially matches recommendations on a “do not send list”
do not disrupt the manifest workflow and allow manifest creators to continue working as usual even if an item is found to match a “do not send list” item

sections.heading: Hypothesis
sections.content:
We believe that if we create a feedback loop at the manifest creation stage that prevents items being sent to e-commerce …  

will achieve an overall reduction of rejected items from not being sent to e-commerce …

We will know we are successful when the average rejection rate across all organizations drops and the general time to process a manifest is reduced by spending less time annotating rejected products.

sections.heading: Success Metrics
content: Reduce average reject rate
Maintain item volume sent from stores

sections.heading: Potential Areas to Explore
content: validation on title field
highlight matching item in-line within the manifest table of items
new column in the manifest table of items: “item preference”
warning banner when match is detected
add “do not send list” into the new manifest page
new table for flagged items

sections.heading: Open Questions
content: Match rate %? How might we distinguish the potential success rate of a match? Example: “Clear pyrex — send white glass pyrex only” = a manifest title of “white picture frame” would match, but with a low match rate, because it matches only 1 of the 7 words from the item preference.
How aware are in-store employees to the admin-applied “do not send list?”

sections.heading: Solution
content: Items are added to manifest – as with the existing experience – when a title is entered into the title field
If an item title fuzzy matches a keyword in any of the items from the “do not send list” then add the item to the “flagged items” table separate from the main manifest table
Allow users to “ignore and add” any flagged items
Any manifest with flagged items at the time of save will trigger a popover modal for users to confirm adding manifest items that match the “do not send list”

gallery.alt: Manifest table with a flagged items table shown separately below it
Confirmation modal and table column shown when saving a manifest with flagged items

sections.content: This generative research was framed to discover and document the landscape of selling books through e-commerce more broadly. Objectives of the research were to uncover the specific needs and goals our customers have regarding the storage, selling, and shipping of media materials. Additionally, the research was designed to learn more about the challenges faced by our users, especially for organizations new to the market.

I led the planning and execution of this research effort to capture the landscape of selling books through e-commerce more broadly. I worked independently to plan the research criteria, recruit and schedule sessions with participants, facilitate customer interviews, and synthesize the findings for leadership.
2 weeks from planning the research and scheduling interviews through final synthesis and recommendations shared with leadership.

content: Discover goals for selling books and media in e-commerce
Uncover challenges with sorting, selling, storage, and shipping
Better understand the sorting and repricing factors in books and media
Learn more about selling used media on Amazon specifically
Understand the differences and similarities of selling each category type of media
Learn how Neatoscan technology determines value through the database and live lookup
4 external interviews with leadership at current customer organizations
2 internal interviews with customer support team members

sections.content: 3–4 members from various teams were selected through interest in being involved in research or team lead identification of participant candidates. Candidates needed to be willing to talk with us and dedicate 30 minutes for an in-person interview, and needed direct experience in engineering, solutions consulting, production, or client experience.

content: What goals regarding selling books did your organization have when starting with Neatoscan?
How have your goals regarding selling books and media changed over time?
How often have you made changes to your accept/reject or repricing rules?
Tell me more about challenges your organization and team have faced regarding sorting, selling, storage, and shipping
What factors are critical to your organization regarding sorting and repricing?
What has the experience of selling on [Marketplace] been like for you and your team?
What are some differences to the approach you take selling [main category type] vs. [secondary category type]?
How does the scanning and sorting look like for your organization?
What are some similarities in the approach you have to selling various category types?
How does Neatoscan technology determine value through both the database and live lookup approaches?
How does the value determination work across various marketplaces?
Why do books (and media) need to be repriced so frequently?
What other alternatives for selling books exist, including without sorting automation?
Individual research interview notes were synthesized into top session takeaways with the format: headline and context
Top takeaways across all research sessions and surveys were grouped and synthesized into top project takeaways
Recommendations were generated from the top project takeaways and framed as new opportunities for vetting by product leadership

image.alt: Synthesis process from session takeaways to project-level recommendations

content: Synthesis of findings from 6 interviews
Reselling books ecosystem diagram
Product audit and documentation of design debt items
Actionable recommendations based on insights from the interviews

image.alt: Overview of research deliverables and recommendations

sections.content: 2 out of 6 new opportunities surfaced from this research's recommendations have been prioritized and added to the product roadmap for design and development cycles. Additionally, 7 design debt items were identified and documented to improve the experience of using Inventory Management for reselling books and media.

sections.subheading: Recommendations from the Research: Become a more proactive customer support team with informed data
content: Data warehouse: set up trend and performance tracking to alert the Neatoscan team when there are downward trends on sales performance
Align to trends of utilizing Amazon less, supporting independent websites and smaller marketplaces for selling books

sections.subheading: Recommendations: Outcome-based system for defining accept/reject and repricing rules
content: Allow users to define the parameters and properties used to sort books
Enable onboarding by defining sorting parameters, flooring price, listing delays, etc.

Increase customer organizations' (especially for onboarding new orgs) comprehension of basic decision factors in accept/reject and repricing rules using plain language and an approachable interface — foundational elements include weight, condition, rank, trends, competition, floor, and minimum profit
Potentially route changes through a form submission sent to the Neatoscan team to process the change request, which could later expand into fully integrated functionality

sections.subheading: Recommendations: A new template-based and additive model for customizing rules
content: Create a Neatoscan-owned and maintained template where updates are automatically applied to all “subscribed” organizations
Continue to have organizations utilize a base template but also enable customization that adds to the template instead of making direct changes to the decision tree
Potentially utilize a rule set and common language to allow users to self-serve within the platform
4 out of 6 research participants mentioned lag and page/tab content load time as a challenge when making changes to accept/reject and repricing rules
Animated transitions between tabs and pages can be disorienting; exploring alternative navigation methods could reduce perceived lag and wait time

sections.subheading: Recommendations: Empower users to troubleshoot unexpected sorting or pricing behavior
content: Make “tracing” more discoverable
Help customers find some answers themselves and reduce the time investment for Neatoscan in tracing and troubleshooting

sections.subheading: Recommendations: Define a system for account changes that is secure, locked, and auditable
content: Attribute changes to a specific user making the changes, not just the account and user logged into the platform
Potentially eliminate the need to remote access users' computers and accounts to make changes
Allow only one user to make editing changes to accept/reject and repricing rules at a time, eliminating changes being overwritten by another user

projects.title: Improving Error Messaging
projects.description: Designed a plain-language error and warning panel in Studio to make render failures easier to understand, scan, and troubleshoot, reducing back-and-forth between the preview and debug log.
projects.detail: Improved Studio’s troubleshooting experience by translating dense debug logs into an approachable, scannable error message panel that helps production personas quickly diagnose issues and know what to do next.

image.alt: The launched Error Message Panel showing plain-language, scannable error and warning messages

sections.content:
The Studio editor includes a preview component that allows users to render the final image they are building to validate the success of the app's configuration. If an image fails to render successfully or as expected, Studio also has a tool for debugging: the debug log.

The challenges with the debug log tool were:

content: Unapproachable by non-technical production personas — a dense and technical log of all information regarding the app
Hard to parse — even for technical production personas, the log was hard to scan and identify critical areas to address
Back and forth with image — users could not view the image and the debug log simultaneously, making it more time consuming to navigate back and forth

sections.content: The majority of Studio users (not just technical users or code editors) would be more successful and faster at diagnosing and troubleshooting rendering issues in Studio if error and warning messages were displayed in plain language that is easy to scan, easy to understand, and easy to act on.

content: Make it easier for any production persona (no matter their level of technical ability) to understand what went wrong when an app fails to render
Reduce the time it takes Studio users to troubleshoot a problem
Increase the scanability of error messaging by emphasizing and highlighting key areas
Help production personas understand what actions to take next to resolve errors

image.alt: The original debug log tool, showing a dense, technical, unformatted list of render information

Early sketch exploring the error message panel layout
Early sketch comparing the before and after states of the error message treatment

caseStudies.title: Building a Product Team Operating System from the Ground Up
caseStudies.description: Built a repeatable product investment operating system: framework, planning cadence, and engineering investment reporting, to make prioritization and roadmap decisions transparent across a multi-product Commerce portfolio.
caseStudies.detail: Built a repeatable product investment operating system: framework, planning cadence, and engineering investment reporting, to make prioritization and roadmap decisions transparent across a multi-product Commerce portfolio.

sections.content: Upright Labs is a B2B SaaS company serving the thrift and secondhand retail industry with web and mobile products for inventory management and e-commerce. After several ownership and organizational changes, the product team now operates within a larger structure while maintaining direct relationships with customers and cross-functional partners in Growth, Customer Experience, and Engineering.

I joined Upright Labs in 2022 as the company’s first design hire, assigned to elevate the products and build a design team. Over the next few years I grew into a strategic product team role with additional responsibilities including roadmap planning, customer communications, internal team rollout coordination, and product direction.

sections.subheading: Building a team and a process
sections.content: I hired and began managing a contracted product designer and defined how our team would collaborate, grow, and own their work. In addition to leading the design team, I also led the organization’s first structured roadmap prioritization process and established decisions grounded in customer feedback, quantitative data, and a repeatable framework rather than opinions. That framework, and the trust it built with engineering and customer-facing teams, became the foundation I’d later scale across the entire organization.

sections.subheading: Designing for many teams, not just one
sections.content: A sudden organizational consolidation brought several previously independent teams under one shared product function. With the merger of 4 unique businesses and a collective 17 product areas, I began co-owning the combined product function. This became the opportunity to scale the existing framework I’d already proven with one team into a full operating system built for four. Additionally we acquired another product designer and our team grew in size and responsibilities, moving from designers to product owners.

content: Defined guiding principles and company/product priorities as shared evaluation criteria for every initiative, advancing strategy, solving meaningful customer problems, benefiting the greatest number of customers, and protecting platform health

Designed a two-part scoring model: a modified RICE framework (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort) calibrated to our signal sources, paired with a customer-assessment layer (cohort, account health, revenue influence, strategic partnerships)
Defined a four-track project-sizing rubric, from quick wins to strategic initiatives, so scope could be evaluated independently of priority
Mapped the full signal-to-solution lifecycle, from customer feedback and internal signals through discovery, delivery, and measured outcomes
Established a single feedback and feature-request intake form across all product areas and audiences (internal teams and customers) along with weekly triage of incoming requests
Hired and managed a contracted product designer, then 2 contract designers
Owned the consolidated product function with initial support from a product analyst and a technical project manager
Built and launched a release communication site for CX and Growth visibility

sections.content:
With several teams now sharing one product function, I evolved my earlier framework into a more rigorous model. Every opportunity, whether a customer request or an internally identified initiative, is evaluated against the same guiding principles before it’s ever scored.

Opportunities that clear that bar are scored two ways: a modified RICE model weighted toward our specific signal sources, and a customer-assessment layer that considers cohort, account health, revenue influence, and strategic partnerships. High-value opportunities with low confidence are routed into discovery before they ever reach the roadmap. I also defined the product goals and created a stable foundation to evaluate initiatives against.

content: Guiding principles and prioritization framework documentation
Process diagram (see below)
Release communications website for internal teams

gallery.alt: Process diagram mapping the full signal-to-solution lifecycle
gallery.caption: Process diagram

gallery.alt: Release communications website used by CX and Growth teams
gallery.caption: The release communications site: conceived, structured, and content-managed by me using a Notion database as a CMS, with AI-assisted implementation, gives CX and Growth teams a living view of what is coming soon, coming next, and coming later, with detail on what is changing, for whom, and why.

content: Built a design team and mentored designers through growth into product owners
Consolidated and standardized product processes
Established a framework for prioritization and roadmap planning
Led the product team through company mergers
Owned product strategy across 17 unique product areas

sections.content:
Product leadership at scale is less about owning decisions and more about designing the conditions for good decisions. As my scope expanded from one product team to four businesses and 17 product areas, I learned that a process only scales when people understand and trust the thinking behind it. I focused on making that thinking explicit: what we value, what signals we trust, how we evaluate tradeoffs, where uncertainty should trigger discovery, and how decisions connect back to customer and business outcomes.

As my role shifted from designing products to designing the systems around them, I became more intentional about creating shared language, reducing ambiguity between teams, and making product reasoning visible to people who weren't directly involved in the work. The result was a useful reminder that good product systems should not make an organization more rigid. They should make it more capable, giving teams a consistent foundation while leaving room for judgment, context, and new information.

caseStudies.title: Leading Through Ambiguity: AI-Supported Retail Workflows

sections.heading: Context
sections.content:
Coaching a product designer to lead discovery on a high-risk, sales-driven initiative and stepping in to protect the design team when the research plan stalled unexpectedly.

This project explored AI-supported workflows to help retail store employees identify products and estimate resale value directly from photos. This capability was already meaningfully impacting customers and their ability to speed up donation processing using the web-based app: pearldive Ama. Seeing a gap in the sales strategy for upselling existing customers using a native app for retail production (Solutions DGR), the Sales team proposed a workflow based on what they believed customers needed: a direct integration between the two systems. Rather than move straight into design, I saw it as an opportunity to test assumptions and ensure we were reducing risk well before development.

content: Identified the need to validate assumptions before committing design or engineering effort
Provided the project framing template used to structure discovery
Coached the project lead through research planning and pivot
Research outreach strategy and messaging
Supported facilitation of the cross-team workshop
Initial discovery, shaping, and framing
Research planning
Led facilitation of the cross-team workshop

sections.heading: Coaching through the first roadblock
sections.content:
Initial project framing was completed by the product designer I manage using the same template I use across all of our projects, documenting the sales team's assumptions clearly enough that we could see how many of them were unverified. In a one-on-one, we discussed research options together and landed on a plan: reach out to existing customers to understand their current product identification and valuation workflows before designing anything new.

The outreach didn't land. Despite a warm handoff from our Customer Experience team, we heard nothing back from our participant pool from the initial ask or the follow-up. We needed to come up with a new plan to maintain momentum.

sections.heading: The pivot
sections.content:
Rather than solve it for her, I used our regular design team sync where myself and two product designers use the space to work through the pivot together. We talked through why customer outreach might be stalling and what alternative paths could still get us reliable signal. The team decided to pivot from external customer interviews to internal team observations and expertise, pulling on what our own Customer Experience and Account Management teams already knew about how customers handled this work today.

From there, I helped the project led curate a cross-team workshop to bring that internal knowledge together and pressure-test the sales team's assumptions directly, but I made a deliberate choice to support facilitation rather than lead it, giving the product designer the room to run the session herself.

sections.heading: Original Plan vs. Pivot
content: Original Plan: Validate assumptions through direct customer interviews, sourced via a CX warm handoff
Pivot: Validate assumptions through internal team expertise and a structured cross-team workshop

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.content:
Friction Risk Surfaced

The Sales team's proposed workflow was found to be largely misaligned with existing operational workflows for processing incoming donations. Clear patterns emerged within the workshop’s workflow mapping activity showing alignment across organizations on the methods used to sort donated goods and prep them for resale. The existing operational workflows were at odds with the solution outlined by the Sales team

Next Steps

The workshop succeeded in surfacing initial risk and pointed the product team toward exploring alternate directions. Catching this friction risk before any design or engineering work began avoided building toward the wrong solution. The project is now moving forward into design, shaped by what we actually validated rather than what was originally assumed.

sections.heading: Learnings
sections.content: The most important leadership decision in this project wasn't the research pivot, it was choosing not to solve the stalled outreach problem myself. I used this project as a coaching moment to bring the design team together to work through it collectively, and let the product designer led her project.

caseStudies.title: Tools for Reselling Books
caseStudies.description: Led discovery and MVP scoping for a book inventory system serving thrift retailers — translating complex operational constraints into a shippable product strategy that supports multiple workflows without forcing change.
caseStudies.detail: Upright Labs needed a fast, reliable ISBN identification and inventory system for thrift retailers — but workflows varied wildly across organizations (store sorting, warehouse QA, fulfillment). I led discovery research with 5 customer interviews and cross-functional validation to understand friction points: slow ISBN lookup, inconsistent pricing confidence, and fulfillment errors in dense shelving.

sections.content:
Secondhand and thrift organizations, like Goodwill and Salvation Army, receive large volumes of donated books every day. This abundant product flow is an asset for mission-based organizations that turn donations into revenue that supports their community programs. The challenge for Upright customers is determining the value of individual donated items at this scale.

The existing ecosystem created friction in a few places:

content: ISBN identification and value lookup could be slow or inconsistent
Workflows varied significantly by org (store sorting vs centralized e-comm teams)
Internet connectivity and “data freshness” constraints affected pricing confidence
Listing and storage expectations (especially inventory locations) could bottleneck throughput
Picking from dense shelving made fulfillment error-prone without better item ID strategies

sections.content: Upright Labs is a B2B SaaS company serving the thrift and secondhand retail industry with web and mobile products for inventory management and multi-channel e-commerce.

content: Define an MVP that would meet functionality and reliability objectives and deliver under a constrained deadline
Enable fast, reliable ISBN identification at scan-time (mobile and web)
Reduce the time and cognitive load required to make a selling destination decision (e-comm vs retail vs salvage vs recycle)
Define an MVP that’s pilot-ready without requiring major operational change
Create a path to scale beyond books (more product categories, marketplaces, and smarter decisioning over time)
Ship a pragmatic pricing approach that protects minimum profit while still supporting sell-through

sections.content: Create a database-first MVP that makes ISBN scanning a “first class action” across Link (mobile) and Lister (web/desktop): quickly identify a book, return trusted product/value data, and guide users through a streamlined workflow to sort, list, store, and fulfill—without over-scoping repricing customization.

I led early discovery, research, scoping, and feature prioritization, translating research insights and operational constraints into a clearly defined MVP and go-to-market direction. My focus was to reduce risk, align stakeholders on tradeoffs, and define a workflow that could realistically succeed in beta environments with varied organization structures.

content: Planned and synthesized discovery work to clarify constraints, validate assumptions, and reduce project risk
Facilitated cross-functional alignment across stakeholders, product, engineering, and customer success teams
Defined project objectives, workflow principles, and scoping tradeoffs
Documented an end-to-end experience and created artifacts that supported build planning
Engineering: feasibility checks, system constraints, and implementation planning
Product and Customer teams: pilot criteria, operational workflow validation, and adoption risk assessment
Understand workflow variability across organizations (store sorting, warehouse QA, fulfillment)
Validate interest in store-level, tool-assisted value identification
Test early hypotheses: minimum profit control, workflow flexibility, purge-to-salvage, and picking support
5 customer interviews
5 internal validation tests
1 cross-functional ideation session
Mobile-first workflows were viable at retail scale; Android patterns aligned with existing Link usage
Flexibility across touchpoints reduced adoption risk more than enforcing one “ideal” workflow
Inventory location timing was a major friction point → supported a “list then store” direction
Fulfillment picking needed a ticket/ID strategy to work in dense shelving environments

sections.subheading: Solution direction: Database-first ISBN identification and lookup
content: Fast scan-time matching via local/cache-backed access
Live lookup for unknown ISBNs with write-through to the cache
Designed to scale beyond books into broader product identification over time
Cached current market value (refreshed on a target cadence)
Estimated shipping cost (dimensions/weight)
Admin-set minimum profit
User-entered condition (plus optional condition details)
Set initial price from market data
Reduce price over time via listing strategies
Never drop below minimum profit
Defer deeper “real-time market trend repricing” customization to later phases

sections.content: Scan ISBN → identify product → destination decision → capture condition → create draft/listing and print ticket → store later (ticket and location) → auto-list eligible items → fulfillment picking supported by ticket/ID

content: A clear MVP strategy anchored on database performance and workflow flexibility
Documented tradeoffs and decisions (especially repricing scope)
Pilot criteria and a rollout/engagement plan to validate in real operations
Design exploration artifacts (batch listing concepts, touchscreen accessibility-forward UI directions, haptic/audio feedback principles, unit tracking taxonomy)
In operationally complex domains, the best MVPs reduce change resistance by supporting multiple valid workflows—not by forcing one “perfect” process.
Clear tradeoff documentation (what’s explicitly out of scope and why) speeds alignment and protects teams from scope creep.

caseStudies.title: Feature: Express List - Redesigning a Core Workflow
caseStudies.description: Reimagined a critical product listing workflow to reduce cognitive load and time-to-list — transforming a long scrolling form into a contextual, card-based interface validated through iterative usability testing.
caseStudies.detail: The existing listing workflow in Upright's web product 'Lister' was a long scrolling form that was difficult to parse and error-prone. Users struggled to identify required fields and complete listings efficiently. I was tasked early in my onboarding to reinvent this critical workflow without disrupting existing users.

sections.content: A core workflow for the web product “Lister” allows users to list a product for sale across multiple marketplaces. Users complete this task by entering details about the product (its dimensions, weight, attributes, price, etc.) including any necessary information determined by the marketplace (eBay, ShopGoodwill, or Shopify). Previous to the redesign, the listing task was completed using a scrolling, long form which was difficult for users to parse and prone to errors.

sections.content: Upright Labs is a business-to-business SaaS company leading the thrift and secondhand retail industry with web and mobile products for inventory management and e-commerce.

content: reduce the average time-to-list metric across all customer organizations
help users identify fields are needed to configure to create a successful listing
avoid disruption of current workflow
focus user-attention and emphasize required fields
reduce cognitive load for users listing products by reducing the amount of decisions
prevent listing errors from happening by restricting submissions with missing values

sections.content: Take a contextual approach to the listing workflow with a redesigned layout that reduces the amount of content displayed and reduces the amount of data entry necessary for a successful listing. “Express List” was designed to increase the average monthly listings across client organizations and a decrease in the average time-to-list metric while also sustaining the average price per item sold.

The challenges faced by the existing listing workflow were shared with me during my hiring process at Upright. I was tasked early in my onboarding to “reinvent” this critical workflow. Our product team was focused on increasing listing efficiency and reducing the time-to-list metric but was hesitant to disrupt users. This project was handled iteratively, and I led efforts to define objectives and find creative solutions to meeting them. The last phase of work, documented here, encompasses the user interface redesign, user testing, final recommendations based on user feedback, and artifacts generated to facilitate collaboration with the engineering lead assigned to development.

content: Iterate on user interface recommendations based on new information

Test the new workflow with a design prototype with internal and external users — identifying and recruiting testing candidates, generating the scenario, task, and script, and creating recruiting, follow-up, and thank-you messaging

sections.subheading: Usability Testing a Clickable Design Prototype
sections.content: I engaged participants in a tasked-based, observational test of the design prototype to gather feedback directly from users about the information architecture, functionality, and new layout of the listing workflow. The learning objective was to validate our early hypothesis and test assumptions about how users would respond.
We believe that by reducing the cognitive load of parsing fields within a full form through only showing fields that are needed, users will (in time) be able to list faster.

content: Users will be looking for specific fields and feel required to enter a value for specific fields
Users will overlook builder templates/product attributes with a “single page form”

content: The side drawer was not discoverable by any participant unless prompted

“Missing” elements/fields seemed to be specific to the workflow of each organization — some found nothing missing, others would not have successful listings without the ability to define scheduling, shipping weight, box size, etc.

Many participants mentioned the listing role as a “final check,” with the processing role handling the majority of the heavy lifting: documenting product condition, dimensions, testing, and details about the item
Improve the discoverability of the side drawer
Make fields flexible, if possible, to have admins define who (permissions) sees what
Adjust the listing strategy to be contextual — if there are multiple listing strategy matches based on the category, display the listing strategy selection field within the workflow
Future iterations: allow linking to complete product attributes
Ensure keyboard navigation across fields and cards is optimized for speed

[Potentially] make some fields (like price) hidden with admin settings or user-permission based — some orgs don't want listers (or some listers) to be able to change the price or set the listing type to buy-it-now

sections.content: The “Express List” feature is currently in development to finish the front-end implementation and final visual design changes. The workflow is a stronger approach to solving for the original productivity efficiency objective. Iterative design cycles created a layout that is future-proof for planned enhancements and additional features as well as responsive and mobile friendly. “Express List” will be launched to all users upon development completion and will co-exist alongside the existing workflow, giving users a choice between the two.

Stepping back into projects with fresh eyes can help to elevate, improve, and strengthen projects with knowledge gained in-between active design cycles. Working iteratively also helped to redefine and focus the objectives of the project and was necessary to designing holistically.
